interest: Tracks Japan's cabinet politics from 1939 to 1944, including reporting via third-country posts after Pearl Harbor.
overview: This file comprises twelve consecutive docket sheets (Form C-0 and 'List of Papers' sheets numbered 37 through 48) from State Department decimal file 894.002 (Internal Affairs of Japan: Cabinet and Ministry), cataloguing documents sub-numbered 410 through 537 from late December 1939 to February 1944. The register meticulously charts the rapid evolution of Japan's government during the transition to and conduct of World War II, spanning the demise of the Abe cabinet, the short-lived tenure of Admiral Mitsumasa Yonai, the rise, reorganizations, and fall of Prince Fumimaro Konoye's second and third cabinets, the ascension of General Hideki Tojo's wartime administration in October 1941, and subsequent wartime shuffles through early 1944. Recorded entries abstract telegrams, despatches, intelligence summaries, and memoranda generated by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo, Allied and neutral listening posts (including Chungking, Bern, London, Vichy, and Kuibyshev), and State Department Far Eastern Affairs analysts, covering critical developments such as the establishment of the Cabinet Intelligence Bureau, the creation of the Greater East Asia Ministry and Foreign Minister Togo's resulting resignation, the attempted assassination of Baron Kiichiro Hiranuma, and the diplomatic impact of Tokyo's ministerial shifts on Japanese-American relations.
